title: Renunciation
hookLine: letting go looks like a cliff from the top. even the Buddha said so.
tomorrow: why would a prince pretend for years that he couldn't speak?

cards: The phone goes in a drawer for one evening, and for the first twenty minutes your hand keeps reaching for it. Is letting go a loss, or something else?
A householder named Tapussa once said that to people like him, giving up pleasures looked like a cliff edge. The Buddha's reply is the surprise. He didn't argue.
He said: before my awakening, I felt the same way.

teach.b: In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha tells Ananda that when he was still seeking, he thought renunciation was good, but his heart didn't leap up at it. It didn't feel like peace. Why?
He hadn't yet seen the drawbacks of what he was holding, or tasted what letting go gives. When he did, his heart leapt.
So the honest answer to the hook: letting go feels like loss until you've seen both sides. The word for this perfection is nekkhamma, renunciation, the third of the ten.
It covers the big letting go, leaving home to be a monk or nun. It also covers small ones.
In the Majjhima Nikaya, the Buddha says that before his awakening he sorted his thoughts into two kinds. On one side, thoughts of craving, ill will and cruelty.
On the other, thoughts of renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness. When a craving thought came, he noticed where it led, harm to himself and others, and it faded.

teach.h: LEAVE THE SMALL FOR THE GREAT.
teach.b: The Dhammapada puts the trade simply: if leaving a small pleasure shows you a great one, the wise leave the small.
That's renunciation for an ordinary week. Not a cliff. A trade you have to see before it makes sense.

how: Renunciation takes many forms among Buddhists: monks and nuns leave home, and lay people practice it in smaller ways, by keeping the eight precepts on observance days, simplifying, or setting down one comfort for a time.

o: letting go, a loss until you see what it trades for
a vow to leave your family and never come back
a fast kept to punish yourself for past mistakes

games.q: letting go, in three texts — tap the pairs.
p: before awakening, I felt the same
leave the small pleasure for the great

s: renunciation only means leaving home to become a monk
it covers that, and small letting go too: thoughts of renunciation, one comfort set down.
the Buddha said his heart didn't leap up at renunciation at first
he hadn't yet seen the drawbacks of what he held, or tasted what letting go gives.
letting go is meant to feel like punishment
it feels like loss until both sides are seen; then, the Buddha said, his heart leapt.

games.q: a friend gives up sweets for a month and is miserable and snappy the whole time. going by the Buddha's talk with Ananda, what's missing?
o: more willpower: grit your teeth until it's over.
seeing what the letting go is for; till then it feels like a cliff.
giving up more things, so this one feels smaller.
games.why: his heart didn't leap at renunciation until he'd seen the drawbacks of what he held and what letting go gives.

practice: Choose one small comfort you could set down for the rest of today: the phone at dinner, the snooze button, the second dessert. Picture the moment you'll reach for it, and feel the little pang.
Then picture what fills the space instead, and make a plan for that moment.

wordCard.voice: Nekkhamma: renunciation, letting go, the third perfection. A loss until you see what it trades for.

orig.note: Pali: renunciation, letting go, the third of the ten perfections.

carryVoice: For the road: let it go, and watch what the open hand gets to hold. Three perfections met, seven to come.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 9.41, Tapussa Sutta (renunciation seems like a precipice to householders; before his awakening the Bodhisatta's heart did not leap up at renunciation, because he had not seen the drawbacks of sensual pleasures or the reward of renunciation; when he did, it leapt up)
Majjhima Nikaya 19, Dvedhavitakka Sutta (two kinds of thought: sensual desire, ill will and cruelty; renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness)
Dhammapada 290 (if by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, the wise leave the small)
